plan.audience: Hypothesis: Riga NGO organisers arranging repeated small catered events, initially ten organisers reachable through moderator-approved local groups. Municipal reuse guidance supplies context, not evidence of sourcing pain or customer demand.
plan.payerAndPrice: Hypothesis: the organiser controlling the event budget pays €3 per completed rental for assisted coordination, separately from supplier rental, deposit, cleaning and transport charges. Disclose the fee before measuring interest. No payments are proposed during the first test.
plan.valueProposition: Proposed benefit: receive dated, quantity-checked tableware options with explicit cleaning, collection and return terms. Compare assisted coordination against contacting the same suppliers directly and using venue tableware; do not assume the intermediary adds value.
plan.firstTest: Within seven days and €20 total, seek permission for two supplier listings and verify their full terms. Invite ten NGO organisers through permitted groups. Show direct and assisted options with €3 disclosed. Pass if three distinct organisers request real dated quotes and at least two choose assistance at that fee; otherwise revise or stop.
plan.mvp: Plan only; nothing has been contacted, tested or implemented. Use a private spreadsheet, consent form and manually sent email for two permissioned listings and ten organisers. Track requests, dated inventory, checks, quote versions and status. A separate human checker gates every quote. Suppliers confirm reservations; no instant booking, payment processing, public marketplace or delivery service. Proceed beyond discovery only if the first test passes.
plan.dataAndPrivacy: Obtain supplier permission for each listed field and organiser permission before sharing contact details with a named supplier. Store dates, quantities, area and contact email; avoid guest data. Restrict the ledger to assigned team roles; keep contacts out of code/logs. Propose deletion 30 days after closure, subject to necessary dispute retention. Confirm provider terms and access controls before use.

architecture.why: Prefer a human-operated existing-tool workflow over a custom marketplace. Evaluate permissions and export/deletion settings before selection. Separate Contacts, Listings, Requests, Holds, Checks and O

architecture.tool: Supplier-direct email and venue tableware enquiry

Do not build it in this MVP. The supplied paid-plan minimum is $5 USD/month, a supplier cost rather than validation. Reconsider only if measured repeat volume justifies maintaining a backend instead o

architecture.tool: Separate checker worksheet and human sign-off
architecture.why: Propose s09 as preparer and s20 as checker. Require a quote-version-specific approval with source confirmation timestamps. A preparer cannot approve their own quote; an edit invalidates approval.

loop.trigger: Proposed daily 09:00 Riga review plus each new request or supplier change. Assign a run ID; inspect unfinished prior runs first. Refresh relevant inventory with suppliers; treat availability older than 24 hours as unverified, not bookable stock.
loop.make: s09 would match dates including cleaning turnaround, item counts and collection area. Create a versioned draft showing rental, deposit, cleaning, transport, cancellation and proposed €3 separately. Use request ID + supplier ID + date range + quote version as the outbox deduplication key.
loop.check: s20 would independently compare supplier confirmation with requested quantities, dates, existing holds and all charges/terms. Reject missing or stale fields. Require supplier reconfirmation before reservation; only the ledger owner may allocate a hold, preventing concurrent double allocation.
loop.deliver: After checker approval, send one quote per outbox key through consented email. Record send time and status. Organiser acceptance is not a booking: supplier must confirm a reference and hold expiry. Request both parties' completion confirmation before marking completed or proposing a fee.
loop.exceptionOwner: s09 would own stale stock, disputes, missed runs and delivery failures. Retry supplier contact once after 24 hours; expire after 48 hours. For ambiguous email sends, inspect Sent before retrying. Freeze conflicting holds, notify affected parties, and escalate disputed terms to s20; never promise a refund or inventory without authority.

weeks.goal: Test sourcing pain and fee preference before building.
tasks: Prepare consent wording, request brief and direct-versus-assisted comparison; seek group moderator permission.
Seek two supplier listing permissions and written dated quantities, prices, deposits, cleaning, delivery and cancellation terms.
Run the ten-organiser invitation test within €20; log distinct responses and fee choices without collecting payment.
Stop or revise if supplier verification or demand thresholds fail; do not treat quote interest as purchase validation.

weeks.goal: If discovery passes, prepare the smallest controlled workflow.
tasks: Configure the private ledger, form and manual outbox; document permissions and deletion procedure.
Define requested, drafted, checked, sent, accepted, supplier-confirmed, completed, cancelled and expired states.
Assign s09 as operator/exception owner and s20 as independent checker; block self-approval.
Use synthetic records to rehearse stale availability, overlapping holds, changed quotes, duplicate intake and uncertain sends.

weeks.goal: Propose a bounded, human-run quote pilot.
tasks: Only with consent, process up to five dated requests using daily inventory refresh and checker sign-off.
Compare assisted coordination with direct booking and venue provision; log organiser reasons and human minutes.
Reconfirm supplier availability before any reservation; record supplier booking reference rather than claiming automatic booking.
Keep payments outside this pilot; record stated €3 preference separately from any future paid conversion.

weeks.goal: Review reliability, repeat intent and economic feasibility.
tasks: Audit every quote against supplier evidence and every send against its deduplication key.
Ask consenting organisers about their next event and preferred route; count a dated repeat request separately from general enthusiasm.
Calculate handling time, acquisition spend and hypothetical contribution; include cancellations and disputes.
Choose stop, narrow or continue. Automate reminders only if the manual loop passes; defer marketplace and payment development.

economics.hypothesis: The proposed €3 completion fee might support lightweight coordination only if handling time and acquisition costs are very low. Fee preference, completion, repeat usage and revenue remain unvalidated.
economics.costAssumptions: Planning assumptions: €20 total discovery budget, €12/hour operator opportunity cost and €0.30 per completion contingency for tools/administration. No payment processor selected; its fees remain unknown. Cloudflare's supplied $5/month paid minimum is an alternative cost, not required MVP spending.
economics.unitEconomics: Illustration, not results: €3 minus 5 minutes at €12/hour (€1) minus €0.30 leaves €1.70 before acquisition, payment fees, tax and disputes. At 15 minutes, contribution is -€0.30 before those costs. If €20 acquired three eventual completions, €6.67 acquisition cost each would exceed the fee.
unknowns: Actual supplier rental prices, deposits and liability allocation.
Completion rate, accepted paid fee, repeat frequency and acquisition cost.
Human minutes including checking, failed matches and disputes.
Payment collection costs, tax treatment, refunds and who bears cancellation losses.

tests.hypothesis: NGO organisers prefer €3 assistance over direct booking for dated needs.
tests.test: Human invites ten organisers after obtaining two permissioned, verified listings; presents comparable assisted, direct and venue options with all known charges. No payment collected.
tests.pass: Within seven days, three distinct organisers request dated quotes and at least two explicitly prefer assistance at €3.
tests.fail: Either threshold is missed, two verified listings cannot be obtained, or interest disappears when the fee is disclosed. Revise or stop; do not infer paid conversion.

tests.hypothesis: The separate checker and ledger prevent unsafe or duplicate releases.
tests.test: Human runs eight synthetic cases: stale stock, short quantity, missing cleaning term, date overlap, duplicate request, repeated send, changed approved quote and missed daily run.
tests.pass: All unsafe drafts are blocked; no duplicate send or conflicting allocation occurs; every case has an owner and auditable outcome.
tests.fail: Any unsafe release, duplicate send, conflicting hold or unowned exception. Repair and rerun before any external quote pilot.

tests.hypothesis: Assisted quotes can be reliable with little enough human work for a €3 fee.
tests.test: After earlier gates pass, time up to five consented requests, including preparation, checking, follow-up and failure handling; independently audit all sent quotes.
tests.pass: At least three quotes delivered, every quote verified, and average total handling at most five minutes per processed request. Treat this as a provisional threshold, not profitability proof.
tests.fail: Any unverified quote or average handling above five minutes; simplify, change the price hypothesis or stop rather than automate the loss.

risks: Municipal reuse guidance supports relevance, not demand for an intermediary.
Suppliers may decline listing permission or be unable to provide reliable dated inventory.
Direct supplier booking or venue stock may dominate the assisted option.
Cleaning, breakage, delivery and deposit disputes may overwhelm a €3 fee.
A spreadsheet hold is not a supplier reservation; stale confirmations can cause double booking.
Role separation requires two available humans; without a checker, quotes must wait.
unknowns: No customer contact, test, user activity, payment, deployment or implementation has occurred.
Which NGO organisers have recurring unmet needs and authority to pay?
Can two suppliers supply permissioned listings with complete dated terms?
What contractual, privacy and consumer obligations would apply before paid operation?

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > [!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > [!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).
evidence.scope: Supplier/tool evidence only; not customer demand or validation.
evidence.quote: You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows.

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > [!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).
evidence.scope: Supplier/tool evidence only; not customer demand or validation.
evidence.quote: You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows.

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > [!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).
evidence.scope: Supplier/tool evidence only; not customer demand or validation.
evidence.quote: You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows.

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > [!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).
evidence.scope: Supplier/tool evidence only; not customer demand or validation.
evidence.quote: You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows.

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > [!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).
evidence.scope: Supplier/tool evidence only; not customer demand or validation.
evidence.quote: You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows.

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > [!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).

records.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
records.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > [!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).

plan.audience: Hypothesis: ten consenting adult friends from one Riga dorm, recruited by a human organizer through a permitted dorm channel. Preferred language, availability and accessibility needs must be established, not assumed.
plan.payerAndPrice: Proposed participant price: €0. No payer is validated. Defer sponsor outreach and payment integration until repeat participation and differentiation pass; any later sponsor price requires a separate test.
plan.valueProposition: Hypothesis: one weekly beginner-friendly outdoor card reduces planning effort versus arranging a walk. Include a 20-minute activity, meeting window, verified location, clear instructions and an equipment-free option. The city facility announcement establishes neither public access nor demand.
plan.firstTest: Within seven days, a human would invite ten consenting adults to two manually checked activities on separate days. Proposed pass: six attend the first and four of those return for the second. Cap incremental cash at €0 and organizer time at four hours. No invitations, tests or implementation have occurred.
plan.mvp: Plan only: one dorm, ten adults, one weekly card and daily internal condition review. Week-one repeat test uses two cards. Use a shared planning sheet, reusable card template and consented existing messaging channel; no app, accounts, payments or autonomous publishing. A different human checks dated access and conditions before founder approval. Suppress uncertain venues; offer a verified equipment-free alternative or cancel. Log delivery, attendance and voluntary feedback. Automate nothing unless manual evidence justifies it.
plan.dataAndPrivacy: Ask permission separately for invitations, attendance tracking and feedback; do not scrape dorm lists. Keep aliases and consent status in a restricted sheet; contacts stay in the organizer's existing channel. Collect no health details, room numbers or live location. Checker sees cards, not contacts. Honor withdrawal; delete identifiable logs within 30 days after week four. Publish only aggregate results.

architecture.tool: Existing shared spreadsheet and card template, proposed
architecture.why: Choose manual rows over a custom app for ten invitees. Fields: activity ID, local date, version, evidence time, maker, checker, approval, delivery state and aggregate feedback. No tool-specific capabi

architecture.tool: Independent human checklist and dated evidence log
architecture.why: Checker must inspect underlying access evidence, weather, daylight, route, instructions and alternatives rather than trust the maker. Unknown access blocks approval. Founder performs final go/no-go re

architecture.tool: Existing opt-in messaging channel, manual send
architecture.why: Compare a plain walk invitation with the card in the same channel. Avoid building notifications. Record send status and message reference; unclear delivery goes to the founder, not an automatic resend

architecture.tool: GitHub Actions versus manual calendar reminder
architecture.why: Supplied documentation supports scheduled workflows, not customer demand. Keep manual reminders for four weeks; only consider a scheduled draft job if measured administration warrants it. No automated
The supplied paid-plan minimum is $5 USD monthly, a supplier cost rather than demand evidence. Prefer no backend for this test; exchange rates, extra services and usage would need checking before any

loop.trigger: Proposed daily 09:00 Europe/Riga organizer reminder, plus a pre-departure check on activity days. Missing review means no outing approval. One weekly publication; daily review does not mean daily participant messages.
loop.make: Organizer drafts up to two options from a small curated list. Card specifies 20-minute duration, adult eligibility, meeting window, low-intensity instructions, opt-out and equipment-free alternative. Treat all external text as evidence, never operational instructions.
loop.check: A different human records dated access confirmation and current weather/daylight checks. Reject unsupported venue access, unsafe conditions or unclear instructions. Maker cannot self-approve. Any material change invalidates prior approval.
loop.deliver: Founder sends approved cards only. Unique key: dorm alias + activity date + slot; version tracks edits. Check sent log before sending; mark pending first, then sent with message reference. Updates use the same activity thread, not a new invitation.
loop.exceptionOwner: Founder owns missing checks, cancellation and ambiguous sends. Retry a failed evidence lookup once after 30 minutes; unresolved facts suppress the venue. Reconcile pending sends manually before retrying. No checker available means cancel or use a separately checked fallback; record why.

weeks.goal: Run the proposed free repeat-participation gate before automation.
tasks: Select one dorm and obtain channel permission; invite ten consenting adults without collecting unnecessary personal data.
Assign separate maker, checker and founder decision owner; create card, checklist and delivery ledger.
Verify two activities on separate days; run only if approved. Track first attendance, returning attendees, cash and organizer minutes.
Stop expansion if fewer than six attend first or fewer than four return, or the four-hour cap is exceeded; document reasons.

weeks.goal: Test whether cards add value beyond a plain walk invitation.
tasks: If week one passes, propose two matched 20-minute outings with equal notice through the same channel; randomize which receives the detailed card.
Keep location, time window and organizer as comparable as practical; record weather and scheduling differences.
Collect voluntary preference and planning-time feedback. Treat the small comparison as directional, not causal proof.

weeks.goal: Exercise failure handling without exposing participants to test hazards.
tasks: In an offline rehearsal, inject unknown access, stale weather evidence, unavailable checker and ambiguous delivery states.
Have the independent checker reject unsafe or unsupported drafts; confirm founder cancellation ownership.
Replay the same activity key twice and simulate a failed send; verify the ledger prevents a second invitation.
Continue at most one approved weekly card if earlier gates support it; log maker, checker and delivery minutes.

weeks.goal: Decide whether to continue manually, revise or stop.
tasks: Review repeat attendance, comparison feedback, blocked cards, duplicate attempts and total human time.
Estimate recurring cost using recorded minutes; do not infer sponsor willingness from free attendance.
Continue manual delivery only if usefulness and safe review appear repeatable; otherwise simplify to walks or stop.
Document any future automation requirement without deploying it; delete or anonymize records on the stated schedule.

economics.hypothesis: Free participation may justify a small manual wellbeing activity, not yet a business. Proposed four-week incremental cash budget is €0 using already available tools; sponsor revenue is untested and excluded.
economics.costAssumptions: Week-one labor cap: four hours; proposed later cap: one hour weekly, seven hours total. At an illustrative €15/hour opportunity cost, total labor is €105. Assumes volunteer time, no travel purchases, equipment, paid software or payment fees.
economics.unitEconomics: Revenue per participant: €0. At four retained participants, illustrative four-week labor cost is €26.25 each (€105/4), with cash contribution €0 before labor. This is a scenario, not an observed result; acquisition and checking time must be measured.
unknowns: Actual organizer and checker minutes, including recruitment and cancellations.
Whether existing tools and suitable nearby locations permit a genuinely €0 incremental test.
Whether any organization would fund ongoing labor; no sponsor interest is established.
Payments and refunds are out of scope; any later paid offer needs separate fee and refund assumptions.

tests.hypothesis: Ten invited adults will show repeat participation without purchases.
tests.test: Human organizer invites ten consenting adults to two checked activities within seven days; count attendance by alias and log all organizer minutes.
tests.pass: At least six attend first and at least four of those return for second; incremental cash €0 and organizer time at most four hours.
tests.fail: Any threshold is missed, or checks cannot establish a suitable outing. Revise or stop rather than automate.

tests.hypothesis: Cards offer more useful planning support than a plain walk invitation.
tests.test: After the first gate, compare two matched outings through the same channel, randomizing card order. Ask attendees who saw both invitations which format helped and why; record preparation time.
tests.pass: At least six give feedback, at least four prefer the card for a concrete planning reason, and card preparation adds no more than 15 minutes.
tests.fail: Any threshold is missed; favor plain invitations or repeat a better-matched comparison rather than claim differentiation.

tests.hypothesis: Independent review and a delivery ledger block unsafe drafts and duplicate sends.
tests.test: Human-run offline rehearsal: unknown access, stale conditions, missing checker, failed send and duplicate activity key. No participant receives rehearsal messages.
tests.pass: All unsafe or unchecked cases are blocked; duplicate replay produces zero extra sends; ambiguous send is held for founder reconciliation.
tests.fail: Any unsafe draft is approved, duplicate is sent or exception lacks an owner; halt delivery and repair the checklist.

risks: A facility announcement is not current permission or a safety inspection; checker must obtain separate dated confirmation.
Friendship, novelty, timing and weather may explain attendance better than cards.
A human checker can share the maker's assumptions; require underlying evidence and explicit unknowns.
Weather, darkness, unequal physical abilities and cancellations may undermine inclusion; permit opting out without explanation.
Manual messaging cannot guarantee atomic delivery; ambiguous status requires reconciliation, not blind retries.
unknowns: Which dorm permits recruitment, and which language and schedule fit consenting adults?
Which locations have confirmed access and appropriate conditions at the intended times?
Can a genuinely separate checker be available within the time budget?
Do residents want weekly cards rather than an ordinary friend-organized walk?
No customer contact, users, payments, deployment, implementation or real-world results have occurred.

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > \[!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).
evidence.scope: Supplier/tool evidence only; not customer demand or validation.
evidence.quote: You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows.

evidence.title: Cloudflare Workers official pricing
evidence.excerpt: The Workers Paid plan includes Workers, Pages Functions, Workers KV, Hyperdrive, and Durable Objects usage for a minimum charge of $5 USD per month for an account. The plan includes increased initial usage allotments, with clear charges for usage that exceeds the base plan. There are no additional charges for data transfer (egress) or throughput (bandwidth). ## Workers Users on the Workers Paid plan have access to the Standard usage model. Workers Enterprise accounts are billed based on the usage model specified in their contract. To switch to the Standard usage model, contact your Account Manager. | | Requests 1, 2, 3, 4 | Duration | CPU time | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | **Free** | 100,000 per day | No charge for duration | 10 milliseconds of CPU time per invocation | | **Standard** | 10 million included per month +$0.30 per additional million | No charge or limit for duration | 30 million CPU milliseconds included per month +$0.02 per additional million CPU milliseconds Max of [5 minutes of CPU time](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/#account-plan-limits) per invocation (default: 30 seconds) Max of 15 minutes of CPU time per [Cron Trigger](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/cron-triggers/) or [Queue Consumer](https://developers.cloudflare.com/queues/configuration/javascript-apis/#consumer) invocation | 1 Inbound requests to your Worker. Cloudflare does not bill for [subrequests](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/#subrequests) you make from your Worker. 2 WebSocket connections made to a Worker are charged as a request, representing the initial `Upgrade` connection made to establish the WebSocket. WebSocket messages routed through a Worker do not count as requests. 3 Requests to static assets are free and unlimited. 4 When [Workers Caching](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/cache/) is enabled, requests served from the Worker's cache are billed at the same per-request rate as requests that invoke the Worker. This includes requests to [static assets](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/static-assets/billing-and-limitations/) and [worker-to-worker invocations](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/pricing/#service-bindings). CPU time is only billed when the Worker runs (on a cache miss or bypass).

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > \[!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).
evidence.scope: Supplier/tool evidence only; not customer demand or validation.
evidence.quote: You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows.

The plan includes increased initial usage allotments, with clear charges for usage that exceeds the base plan. There are no additional charges for data transfer (egress) or throughput (bandwidth). ## Workers Users on the Workers Paid plan have access to the Standard usage model. Workers Enterprise accounts are billed based on the usage model specified in their contract. To switch to the Standard usage model, contact your Account Manager. | | Requests 1, 2, 3, 4 | Duration | CPU time | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | **Free** | 100,000 per day | No charge for duration | 10 milliseconds of CPU time per invocation | | **Standard** | 10 million included per month +$0.30 per additional million | No charge or limit for duration | 30 million CPU milliseconds included per month +$0.02 per additional million CPU milliseconds Max of [5 minutes of CPU time](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/#account-plan-limits) per invocation (default: 30 seconds) Max of 15 minutes of CPU time per [Cron Trigger](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/cron-triggers/) or [Queue Consumer](https://developers.cloudflare.com/queues/configuration/javascript-apis/#consumer) invocation | 1 Inbound requests to your Worker. Cloudflare does not bill for [subrequests](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/#subrequests) you make from your Worker. 2 WebSocket connections made to a Worker are charged as a request, representing the initial `Upgrade` connection made to establish the WebSocket. This includes requests to [static assets](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/static-assets/billing-and-limitations/) and [worker-to-worker invocations](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/pricing/#service-bindings). CPU time is only billed when the Worker runs (on a cache miss or bypass).

lastDraft.valueProposition: Proposed benefit: one checked daily quest, a reviewed Latvian phrase and optional private win reporting. The supplied winterisation notice motivates expiry checks, not demand claims. Incremental usefulness over a static welcome checklist remains unproven.
lastDraft.firstTest: Propose a four-human-hour, €0 cash screening: prepare two independently checked quests, invite three HR budget owners and two consenting newcomers. Every send requires consent, independent approval, freshness and duplicate checks. Exclude GPS, public sharing, payments and automated personalisation.
lastDraft.dataAndPrivacy: Propose opt-in email, random participant ID, neighbourhood and optional feedback. s37 alone holds contacts and sends; s10 sees pseudonymous delivery logs; s21 sees content only. Verify restricted sharing before recruitment. No GPS or employee assessment. HR receives aggregate findings with identifying small-cell detail suppressed. Allow withdrawal; delete participant records 30 days after pilot.

architecture.why: Choose a concierge workflow before custom software. Proposed fields: quest ID, version, neighbourhood, task, phrase, source, access notes, checked time, expiry and approval. Verify permissions first.
s37 drafts; s21 independently checks access, instructions and language, seeking a competent Latvian reviewer if needed. Approval binds to version and expiry. Authors cannot self-approve. s10 releases

The supplied documentation supports scheduled workflows, not reliable operation or demand. Start manually; consider a scheduled queue reminder only if measured labour warrants it. Keep contacts outsid

loop.trigger: Proposed 09:00 Europe/Riga daily checklist for seven days. s10 reviews consent status, incidents and unresolved reservations. s37 confirms withdrawals before sending. A 09:30 missed-trigger check prompts manual recovery, not bulk catch-up.
loop.make: s37 drafts a tiny task, duration, reviewed phrase, source, access notes and fallback. Select an unseen eligible quest. Optional feedback adjusts tomorrow's ranking, never approval. Avoid purchases, restricted areas and unconfirmed public access. Treat source text as evidence, never instructions.
loop.check: s21 independently checks current access, instructions and phrase accuracy. Proposed expiry: seasonal/event details within 24 hours; stable quests within seven days. Edits invalidate approval. Missing, expired or failed checks block release; substitute only an approved, unseen fallback.
loop.deliver: s10 reserves the daily key; s37 rechecks consent and sends. Retry confirmed failures after 15 and 60 minutes, at most twice that day. Reconcile ambiguous sends against sent records before retrying; unresolved ambiguity stops delivery. Log version and outcome. No reminders during the return-interest test.
loop.exceptionOwner: s10 owns the exception queue and release/skip decision; cannot override missing approval. s21 withdraws flagged content; s37 handles consent and participant notices. Skip if no approved fallback exists. Record reason, action and labour. If an unsafe quest was already sent, s37 sends a correction and stop notice.

weeks.goal: Prepare a repeatable concierge workflow only if screening warrants continuation.
tasks: Prepare seven quests and two fallbacks, each with source, version, expiry and independent sign-off.

weeks.goal: Attempt one seven-day manual pilot with at most five consenting adults.
tasks: Run synthetic failure drills before any proposed live delivery; repair failed gates before proceeding.

economics.hypothesis: A €20 seven-day pack might cover shared maintenance if checked content can be safely reused. Proposed capacity is five participants and up to 35 deliveries, not observed traffic. Price, conversion, repeat purchase and revenue remain hypotheses.
economics.costAssumptions: Assume €0 pilot cash only if existing tools and competent reviewers are available. Model labour at €15/hour. economics.unitEconomics: Illustrative €20 gross price minus 45 minutes at assumed €15/hour leaves €8.75 before acquisition, tools, fees, tax and refunds. Eighty labour minutes consume the full gross price. Allocate shared maintenance across actual cohorts; report setup separately. A 45-minute target is unproven.

Tool availability, payment fees, tax treatment and refund exposure.

tests.hypothesis: HR prefers checked quests over municipal links and a curated checklist at €20.
tests.test: Human presents both alternatives to three confirmed HR budget owners in varied order. Ask preference, specific reason and nonbinding willingness to buy the defined seven-day pack. Take no payment.
tests.pass: At least one prefers the quest pack and records willingness to buy at €20 with a specific reason. This is a screening signal, not a sale.
tests.fail: Zero qualifying buyers fails the threshold. Fewer than three interviews is inconclusive and blocks expansion.

tests.hypothesis: Newcomers complete a quest and voluntarily seek another.
tests.test: Two consenting newcomers receive a checked prototype and a clear way to request another quest. Send no reminder for 24 hours. Ask comparative usefulness afterward.
tests.pass: Both complete one quest and at least one independently requests another within 24 hours. Report perceived usefulness separately.
tests.fail: Either threshold is missed. Separate access failure from lack of interest; consider a one-off pack rather than assuming all value is disproven.

tests.hypothesis: Manual gates prevent invalid or duplicate sends within a plausible labour budget.
tests.test: Human rehearses expired approval, edited content, failed access, withdrawal, duplicate trigger, confirmed send failure and ambiguous send. Time a simulated seven-day workflow with allocated shared checking.
tests.pass: All seven cases block, substitute or reconcile correctly; no duplicate occurs; retries obey limits. Projected recurring labour is at most 45 minutes per cohort, with setup separate.
tests.fail: Any invalid, withdrawn-consent or duplicate release; blind ambiguous retry; or labour above target requires revision before expansion.

weeks.goal: Run a bounded discovery pilot, not a launch.

Record optional play reports, missing responses, cash and all team minutes; stop at €20 or six hours.

Collect voluntary repeat reports using the same definition; report nonresponses and distinguish new from returning listeners.

weeks.goal: Decide whether another experiment is warranted.

Listener willingness to pay, sponsor purchasing authority, acquisition cost and acceptable editorial boundaries.

tests.hypothesis: At least four of ten commuters voluntarily return for a distinct episode.
tests.test: A human recruits ten consenting commuters and offers three checked episodes on fixed days within seven days. Each gets a 48-hour response window and identical availability notices, not individual reminders. Optional reports identify episodes played; no reward for listening.

tests.pass: All unsafe cases held, no duplicate authorized, bounded retries logged and every exception owned; clean rehearsals average at most 60 team minutes each.
tests.fail: Any unsafe approval, duplicate authorization, unowned exception or production average above 60 minutes. Fix and repeat before expanding.

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > [!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).
evidence.scope: Supplier/tool evidence only; not customer demand or validation.

planHistory.audience: Hypothesis: culture-curious SSE student commuters want a ninety-second Riga discovery without searching listings. Start with ten consenting volunteers; language and channel remain choices to confirm. No recruitment or listening has occurred.
planHistory.payerAndPrice: Proposed pilot: €0 per listener, founder-funded, with no established payer. No payment infrastructure. Subscription or venue sponsorship would require separate willingness-to-pay tests, not inference from free repeat listening.
planHistory.valueProposition: Proposed benefit: one checked Riga culture story per weekday, with a source link and an optional, date-verified weekend place. Compare against reading the original city listing. The supplied museum listing is an editorial lead, not evidence of demand or reliable daily supply.
planHistory.firstTest: Within seven days, a human founder would invite ten consenting SSE commuters and privately offer three checked episodes plus source links. Cap cash at €20 and total team work at six hours. Pass if four of ten voluntarily play a different episode without an individual reminder; fail otherwise, including inability to recruit or publish within caps.
planHistory.mvp: Plan only: a spreadsheet queue, manual source review, original scripts, human narration and privately shared audio links. Three episodes in week one; conditional weekday production thereafter. No app, scraper, AI voice, payment or recommendation engine. States: candidate, drafted, checked, approved, reserved, sent, held, corrected. Separate approval gates every release; insufficient sources or permissions means no episode.
planHistory.dataAndPrivacy: Seek opt-in for delivery and optional play confirmation separately. Founder alone holds contacts in a restricted file; checker sees pseudonymous IDs only. Store no commute routes or passive tracking. Delete contact and response data 30 days after pilot; retain anonymized totals. Public access is not reuse permission: link sources, write original text, use own narration and no unlicensed media.

loop.trigger: Each proposed weekday morning, researcher s07 reviews dated city leads and the ledger. Canonical URL plus event/date identifies a candidate; reject duplicates and expired events. Receipt excerpts are leads, not sufficient verification of unsupported details.
loop.make: s07 drafts an original ninety-second script with claim-to-source rows and a conditional weekend suggestion. Founder/build s18 records only after script approval. Keep source access date, rights basis, script version and audio version together; do not fill gaps with invented cultural details.
loop.check: Independent checker s29 verifies every factual claim, dates, place, permissions, pronunciation and audio against the approved script. Missing access, ambiguous rights or stale dates means held. Changed scripts or audio invalidate approval. No self-approval; checker absence means skip.
loop.deliver: Founder s18 reserves one release ID and recipient batch in the ledger, checks approval and prior sends, then shares audio plus source links. Mark sent only after confirmation. Retry source access twice that day; retry a failed upload once. For uncertain sends, inspect history before retrying; never blindly resend.
loop.exceptionOwner: Founder s18 owns access failures, duplicate alerts, contact custody and corrections. Checker s29 must approve resolution of factual or rights flags. Hold unresolved items; skip rather than fabricate. If already sent, stop further sharing, withdraw the file where possible and notify recipients with a checked correction.

weeks.goal: Run the bounded repeat-listening screen, not a launch.
tasks: Agree language and channel during consent; preregister repeat definition and six-hour team-work cap.
Set up ledger, restricted contact file and separate checker checklist using dummy data.
Human-invite ten volunteers; make and independently approve three episodes if sources and permissions suffice.
Collect optional pseudonymous play confirmations; report denominator, missing responses, cash and team minutes.

weeks.goal: Test the alternative and operational safety only if week one passes.
tasks: Compare matched audio and original listings with counterbalanced presentation order.
Run a duplicate, stale-date, missing-permission and failed-send drill without contacting participants.
Measure drafting, checking, recording and delivery minutes separately.
If week one fails, interview willing volunteers and revise the format instead of expanding cadence.

weeks.goal: Check whether a weekday rhythm is feasible and still useful.
tasks: Only after demand and safety screens pass, attempt five weekday releases with an explicit skip policy.
Keep a five-item candidate buffer; record rejected leads and reasons rather than lowering verification standards.
Offer one verified weekend suggestion and ask whether it helped; attendance is not assumed.
Audit approvals, duplicate keys, permissions and voluntary repeat reports.

weeks.goal: Decide whether another experiment is justified.
tasks: Compare weeks for repeat listening, missing responses, source yield, errors and total human minutes.
Reconfirm voluntary interest without individual listening reminders; distinguish novelty from sustained use.
Document whether to continue manually, change cadence or stop; automate only a measured bottleneck.
Delete pilot personal data on schedule and publish only anonymized findings with sample limitations.

economics.hypothesis: A free manual pilot may justify further learning if repeat use and production effort both pass. It does not establish a business. Proposed four-week cash ceiling is €50, including week one's €20, conditional on passing screens.
economics.costAssumptions: Planning assumptions: existing devices/accounts, €0 incremental recording cost, no paid acquisition and no participant reward for repeat plays. Verify service terms before use. Value team time at a hypothetical €15/hour; week-one six-hour cap includes recruitment and checking. No fees or refunds at €0.
economics.unitEconomics: At three episodes and six total team hours, imputed labor is €90 plus up to €20 cash: €110 total or €36.67 per episode. At exactly four repeat listeners, cost is €27.50 per repeat listener. These are scenario calculations, not observed costs. Revenue is €0; cost recovery is unproven.
unknowns: Actual recruitment effort, production minutes, hosting charges and permission costs.
Whether enough suitable sources exist without excessive editorial labor.
Whether any listener or sponsor would pay, at what price, and with what acquisition cost.

tests.hypothesis: At least four of ten invited commuters voluntarily return for another story.
tests.test: Human-run week-one pilot: three checked episodes, source links and optional minimal play confirmation. No individual reminder or reward for repeat listening. Record missing responses as no confirmed repeat.
tests.pass: At least four of ten play a different episode within seven days, with recruitment and publication completed within €20 and six team hours.
tests.fail: Fewer than four confirmed repeats, incomplete recruitment/publication or either cap exceeded. Revise rather than claim demand.

tests.hypothesis: Audio offers more value than the existing city listing.
tests.test: If week one passes, offer ten consenting participants matched audio/listing pairs in counterbalanced order. Ask which they would choose for the next commute and why; collect no payment.
tests.pass: At least six of ten choose audio and identify a specific benefit; treat this only as a directional small-sample signal.
tests.fail: Fewer than six choose audio, or choices are missing. Do not expand cadence on repeat-use evidence alone.

tests.hypothesis: The manual approval and ledger controls prevent unsafe or duplicate releases.
tests.test: Before expanded delivery, founder stages five dummy cases: duplicate event, stale date, unclear rights, upload failure and uncertain send. Separate checker reviews; no participant receives drill content.
tests.pass: All unsafe cases held, no duplicate send authorized, retries logged and each exception assigned; three clean episode rehearsals average at most 60 team minutes each.
tests.fail: Any unsafe approval, duplicate authorization, unowned exception or production average above 60 minutes. Fix and repeat before expansion.

risks: Small, single-school recruitment may produce politeness or novelty effects rather than durable listening.
Dated city listings support leads, not historical interpretation, reuse rights or current event availability.
Daily production may exhaust suitable material or overwhelm independent checking.
Self-reported plays are incomplete evidence; avoid covert tracking to compensate.
A weekend suggestion may be inaccessible, cancelled or irrelevant; verify details and avoid guaranteeing availability.
unknowns: No customer contact, tests, users, payments, deployment or implementation have occurred.
Preferred language, channel, commute context and audio accessibility needs remain untested.
Tool access controls, storage terms and source permissions require human verification.
No evidence yet supports launch, paid pricing, sponsor demand or dependable daily story supply.

evidence.title: GitHub Actions official schedule documentation
evidence.excerpt: ## `on.schedule` You can use `on.schedule` to define a time schedule for your workflows. Use [POSIX cron syntax](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/utilities/crontab.html#tag_20_25_07) to schedule workflows to run at specific times. By default, scheduled workflows run in UTC. You can optionally specify a timezone using an [IANA timezone string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones) for timezone-aware scheduling. Scheduled workflows run on the latest commit on the default branch. The shortest interval you can run scheduled workflows is once every 5 minutes. > [!NOTE] > For schedules that set `timezone` to a time zone that observes daylight saving time (DST), during DST spring-forward transitions, scheduled workflows in skipped hours advance to the next valid time. For example, a 2:30 AM schedule advances to 3:00 AM. Cron syntax has five fields separated by a space, and each field represents a unit of time. ```text ┌───────────── minute (0 - 59) │ ┌───────────── hour (0 - 23) │ │ ┌───────────── day of the month (1 - 31) │ │ │ ┌───────────── month (1 - 12 or JAN-DEC) │ │ │ │ ┌───────────── day of the week (0 - 6 or SUN-SAT) │ │ │ │ │ * * * * * ``` You can use these operators in any of the five fields: | Operator | Description | Example | | -------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | \* | Any value | `15 * * * *` runs at every minute 15 of every hour of every day. | | , | Value list separator | `2,10 4,5 * * *` runs at minute 2 and 10 of the 4th and 5th hour of every day. | | - | Range of values | `30 4-6 * * *` runs at minute 30 of the 4th, 5th, and 6th hour. | | / | Step values | `20/15 * * * *` runs every 15 minutes starting from minute 20 through 59 (minutes 20, 35, and 50). | This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 AM in the America/New\_York timezone every Monday through Friday: ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1-5' timezone: "America/New_York" ``` A single workflow can be triggered by multiple `schedule` events. Access the `schedule` event that triggered the workflow through the `github.event.schedule` context. This example triggers the workflow to run at 5:30 UTC every Monday-Thursday, and 17:30 UTC on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but skips the `Not on Monday or Wednesday` step on Monday and Wednesday. ```yaml on: schedule: - cron: '30 5 * * 1,3' - cron: '30 5,17 * * 2,4' jobs: test_schedule: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Not on Monday or Wednesday if: github.event.schedule != '30 5 * * 1,3' run: echo "This step will be skipped on Monday and Wednesday" - name: Every time run: echo "This step will always run" ``` For more information about `schedule` events, see [Events that trigger workflows](/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule).
